items.title: Get It? Describe an event, different from a campfire, in which more than one form of energy is evident.

answer.html: An electric blender making a smoothie: electrical energy is converted to the kinetic energy of the spinning blades and fruit, plus sound (the whirring) and thermal energy (the motor and the mixture warm up slightly). A rocket launch (chemical to kinetic, thermal, sound and light) also works.

items.title: Get It? Why does a cyclist moving at 12 m/s have nine times the translational kinetic energy of the same cyclist moving at 4 m/s?

body.html: 𝐾𝐸<sub>trans</sub> =<sup> </sup><sup>12</sup>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup>; the same mass 𝑚 is used, so the ratio depends on 𝑣<sup>2</sup>.

answer.html: Tripling the speed multiplies 𝑣<sup>2</sup> by 3<sup>2</sup> = 9, so the kinetic energy is nine times as large.

items.title: CCC (Systems and System Models): Describe a mathematical model of an energy calculation for a swinging playground swing, and state its limits.

body.html: Pick a model, state its assumptions, and compare with reality.

answer.html: Example: model a child on a swing with 𝑚𝑔ℎ=<sub> </sub><sub>12</sub>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> at the bottom and no friction, so the swing would reach the same height on every swing forever. Evidence the model is limited: a real swing gradually stops unless someone pumps it, because air resistance and friction at the pivot convert mechanical energy to thermal energy, which the simple model ignores. Present it to a peer by stating the model, its assumptions (no friction, point mass), a prediction (constant amplitude), and the observation that contradicts it.

items.title: Get It? Describe the energy transformations in a wind turbine on a hilltop.

answer.html: Moving air has kinetic energy. It pushes on the blades and transfers energy to their rotational kinetic energy. The spinning shaft turns a generator, which converts it to electrical energy (with some thermal energy and sound lost along the way).

items.title: Figure 16, Analyze: A ball sits on a table. Where else might you place the reference level for its gravitational potential energy?

answer.html: Anywhere convenient, for example at the floor, at the tabletop, or at the ceiling. Changing the reference level changes the numerical value of GPE (and could make it negative) but not the change in GPE or the physics of the motion.

items.title: Get It? Define elastic potential energy using a compressed pogo-stick spring as your example.

answer.html: Elastic potential energy is the energy stored in a system because an elastic object has been stretched, compressed or bent, that is, because of a change in its shape. A compressed pogo-stick spring stores elastic potential energy that is released as the spring pushes the rider upward.

items.title: Get It? Why do we need to understand the interactions inside a battery to predict how much energy it can store?

answer.html: The system's total energy depends on the interactions of its parts (here, the chemical bonds and charges inside the cell). Without knowing those interactions we cannot build a mathematical model to predict how much energy can be stored or released. Understanding the subprocesses lets us account for all the energy in the system.

items.title: CCC (Energy and Matter): Make an energy-flow poster outline for a ski jumper from the start gate to the landing.

answer.html: Poster outline (sequence): (1) Start gate: the jumper at the top of the ramp has mostly gravitational potential energy. (2) Down the ramp: gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy (evidence: increasing speed; a little becomes thermal energy from friction and air drag). (3) Takeoff and flight: kinetic and gravitational potential energy trade back and forth as the jumper rises and falls (evidence: the arc of the flight). (4) Landing: the snow does negative work, turning the kinetic energy into thermal energy and sound (evidence: the jumper slows, the snow compacts, the thud). Total energy is conserved throughout.

items.title: Practice Problems after Example Problem 4 (gravitational potential energy) Problem 1. A 3.20-kg pumpkin sits on the ground beside a table whose top is 0.95 m above the ground. Find the pumpkin-Earth GPE using the tabletop as the reference level.

body.html: 𝑚= 3.20 kg, the ground is 0.95 m below the tabletop ( ℎ= −0.95 m).
𝐺𝑃𝐸= 𝑚𝑔ℎ, with ℎ measured from the reference level (negative below it).

answer.html: 𝐺𝑃𝐸= −30 J (negative because the pumpkin is below the reference level)

items.title: 2. You slowly lower a 15.0-kg bucket of paint 2.40 m down from a scaffold. How much work do you do on the bucket?

body.html: Lowering slowly, your upward force equals the weight 𝑚𝑔, but the displacement is downward, so you do negative work.

answer.html: 𝑊= −3.53 × 10<sup>2</sup> J (the bucket's GPE decreases by this amount)

items.title: 3. A 1.6-kg dictionary is moved from a 0.75-m-high table to a 1.85-m-high shelf. What is its GPE relative to the table?

body.html: Height above the table = 1.85 −0.75 = 1.10 m.

answer.html: 𝐺𝑃𝐸= 17 J

items.title: 4. A 3.4-kg flowerpot falls 5.8 m from a balcony to the sidewalk. What is the change in the pot-Earth GPE?

body.html: 𝛥𝐺𝑃𝐸= 𝑚𝑔(ℎ<sub>𝑓</sub>−ℎ<sub>𝑖</sub>); the pot moves down, so the change is negative.

answer.html: 𝛥𝐺𝑃𝐸= −1.9 × 10<sup>2</sup> J (the system loses this potential energy, which becomes kinetic energy)

items.title: 5 (Challenge). A 16.4-kg crate is lifted onto a 1.3-m-high bench, slid 3.5 m along the bench, and then lowered back to the floor. Find the change in the system's energy during each stage and in total.

body.html: GPE depends only on height. The crate starts and ends at rest on the floor.

answer.html: The crate-Earth system's energy increases by about 2.1 × 10<sup>2</sup> J while lifting, does not change while sliding (no friction), and decreases by 2.1 × 10<sup>2</sup> J while lowering. The total change in the system's energy is 0 J.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress Problem 1. A spring-loaded ball launcher fires a ball straight up (system: ball, spring, Earth). The spring starts compressed with the ball at rest. Sketch bar graphs and describe the energy at (a) the start, (b) the instant the spring reaches its natural length and releases the ball, and (c) the top of the flight; (d) summarize the forms of energy involved.

question.html: Energy bar graphs (reference level at the compressed ball's starting height; relative bar heights): Instance Elastic PE Gravitational PE Kinetic energy (a) Spring compressed, ball at rest tall bar 0 0 (b) Spring at natural length, ball leaving 0 small large, nearly all the energy (c) Top of flight 0 tall bar (equals the original EPE) 0

answer.html: All of the system's energy is elastic potential energy (EPE bar only). Answer (b): The spring has released all of its EPE; the KE bar is large, plus a small GPE bar because the ball has risen a little. KE plus GPE equals the original EPE. Answer (c): At the top the ball is momentarily at rest, so KE is 0 and all of the original energy is now GPE (the GPE bar equals the original EPE bar). Answer (d): Energy shows up as stored energy of shape (elastic PE), as motion (kinetic), and as stored energy due to height (gravitational PE). It is transformed from EPE to KE to GPE while the total stays constant (a bit leaks to thermal energy and sound).

items.title: 2a. A 40.0-kg crate hangs from a helicopter hovering 310 m above the ground. Find its GPE with the reference level at the ground.

body.html: 𝐺𝑃𝐸= 𝑚𝑔ℎ.

answer.html: 𝐺𝑃𝐸= 1.22 × 10<sup>5</sup> J

items.title: 2b. The helicopter descends and the crate is now 120 m above the ground. What is the change in GPE?

answer.html: 𝛥𝐺𝑃𝐸= −7.45 × 10<sup>4</sup> J

items.title: 2c. What motions and interactions does this system depend on?

answer.html: The crate's motion (its speed, giving kinetic energy) and the gravitational interaction between the crate and Earth (which depends on their separation and gives GPE). Earth's tiny motion is negligible. (Air resistance, if included, adds thermal-energy interactions with the air.)

items.title: 3. A heavy flywheel is spun up so it turns 1.5 times as fast. Compare its new angular momentum and rotational kinetic energy with the old values.

body.html: 𝐿= 𝐼𝜔 and 𝐾𝐸<sub>rot</sub> =<sup> </sup><sup>12</sup>𝐼𝜔<sup>2</sup>, with 𝐼 unchanged.
𝐿<sub>𝑓</sub>/ 𝐿<sub>𝑖</sub>= 1.5𝜔/ 𝜔= 1.5; 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>/ 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>= (1.5𝜔)<sup>2</sup> / 𝜔<sup>2</sup> = 2.25.

answer.html: The angular momentum becomes 1.5 times as large, and the rotational kinetic energy becomes 2.25 times as large.

items.title: 4a. Priya aims a leaf blower at a lab cart on a frictionless air track, and the blower pushes with a constant force 𝐹 over a distance 𝑑. Describe the work and the cart's energy using a bar graph.

body.html: Constant horizontal force through a displacement does work 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑 on the cart; 𝑊= 𝛥𝐾𝐸. Assume the cart starts at rest.

answer.html: The blower's air does positive work 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑 on the cart. The bar graph shows 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>= 0, plus a work bar 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑, equals a final bar 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝐹𝑑 of the same height. The cart's kinetic energy increases by exactly the work done.

items.title: 4b. Repeat with a cart of three times the mass, same force and same distance.

body.html: 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑 is unchanged. So 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝑊 is also unchanged. With three times the mass, 𝑣= √2𝐾𝐸/ 𝑚 is smaller by a factor of 1 / √3 ≈0.58.

answer.html: The work done and the final kinetic energy are the same as in part a; only the cart's speed is smaller (by a factor of 0.58).

items.title: 4c. Describe parts a and b in terms of impulse and momentum.

body.html: Impulse = 𝐹𝛥𝑡= 𝛥𝑝, and 𝑝= √2𝑚𝐾𝐸. For the same 𝐾𝐸, the heavier cart has 𝑝 larger by √3 . It accelerates at one-third the rate, so it covers the distance in a time longer by √3 .

answer.html: In both parts the force is the same, but the heavier cart is pushed for a longer time (𝛥𝑡 larger by a factor √3 ). The impulse 𝐹𝛥𝑡 and the final momentum are therefore larger by √3 ≈1.73 for the heavier cart, even though the final kinetic energy is the same.

items.title: Get It? Describe an event in which more than one form of energy is evident

answer.html: A campfire: the wood's chemical energy is converted to thermal energy (heat you feel), radiant energy (light), and sound (crackling). A fireworks display or a roller coaster (kinetic, gravitational potential, thermal, sound) also works.

items.title: Get It? Why does a car at 20 m/s have four times the translational kinetic energy of the same car at 10 m/s?

body.html: 𝐾𝐸<sub>trans</sub> =<sup> </sup><sup>12</sup>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup>; the same mass 𝑚 is used, so the ratio depends on 𝑣<sup>2</sup>.

answer.html: Doubling the speed multiplies 𝑣<sup>2</sup> by 2<sup>2</sup> = 4, so the kinetic energy is four times as large.

items.title: CCC (Systems and System Models): a mathematical model of an energy calculation, and its limits

body.html: Pick a model, state its assumptions, and compare with reality.

answer.html: Example: model a skater gliding on ice with 𝐾𝐸=<sub> </sub><sub>12</sub>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> and no friction, so she would coast forever. Evidence the model is limited: real skaters slow down and stop, because friction and air resistance convert kinetic energy to thermal energy, which the simple model ignores. items.title: Get It? Describe the energy transformations in the dam at the beginning of the module

answer.html: Water stored high behind the dam has gravitational potential energy. As it flows down through the dam, that energy becomes kinetic energy of the moving water. The water spins turbines, transferring kinetic energy to rotational kinetic energy of the generator, which converts it to electrical energy (with some thermal energy and sound lost along the way).

items.title: Figure 16, Analyze: Where else might you place the reference level?

answer.html: Anywhere convenient, for example at the ground, at a table top, or at the ball's launch point. Changing the reference level changes the numerical value of GPE (and could make it negative) but not the change in GPE or the physics of the motion.

items.title: Get It? Define elastic potential energy

answer.html: Elastic potential energy is the energy stored in a system because an elastic object (a spring, bow, rubber band, or trampoline) has been stretched, compressed or bent, that is, because of a change in its shape.

items.title: Get It? Why do we need to understand the interactions in a process or subprocess to understand a system?

answer.html: The system's total energy depends on the motions and interactions of its parts (for example, the forces holding a nucleus together or the chemical bonds in food). Without knowing those interactions we cannot build a mathematical model to predict how much energy can be stored or released. Understanding the subprocesses lets us account for all the energy in the system.

items.title: CCC (Energy and Matter): energy flow poster for a pole-vaulter-track system

answer.html: Poster outline (sequence): (1) Run-up: chemical energy from the vaulter's body becomes kinetic energy. (2) Plant and bend: kinetic energy becomes elastic potential energy in the bent pole (evidence: the visibly curved pole, the vaulter slowing). (3) Pole straightens: elastic potential energy becomes gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy as the vaulter rises (evidence: increased height). (4) At the top: mostly gravitational potential energy (the vaulter nearly stops). (5) Fall and landing: gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy, and the landing pad does negative work, turning it into thermal energy and sound (evidence: the pad compresses, the thud). Total energy is conserved throughout.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress Problem 1. Jumping spring toy (system: toy, spring, Earth): bar graphs and description

question.html: Energy bar graphs (reference level at the compressed toy's starting height; relative bar heights): Instance Elastic PE Gravitational PE Kinetic energy (a) Pushed down, spring compressed, at rest tall bar 0 0 (b) Spring expands, toy leaves ground and jumps decreasing to 0 as the spring reaches natural length small, growing grows to a maximum when the spring is fully extended (c) Top of flight 0 tall bar (equals the original EPE) 0

answer.html: All of the system's energy is elastic potential energy (EPE bar only). Answer (b): EPE is converting to KE (and some GPE); the EPE bar shrinks while the KE bar grows. When the spring reaches natural length, EPE is 0 and KE plus a little GPE equals the original EPE. Answer (c): At the top the toy is momentarily at rest, so KE is 0 and all of the original energy is now GPE (the GPE bar equals the original EPE bar). Answer (d): Energy shows up as stored energy of shape (elastic PE), as motion (kinetic), and as stored energy due to height (gravitational PE). Work you do on the spring first stores EPE; it is transformed to KE and then to GPE while the total stays constant (a bit leaks to thermal energy and sound).

items.title: 4a. Karl's air hose moves a puck a fixed distance on a frictionless air table

body.html: Constant horizontal force through a displacement does work 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑 on the puck; 𝑊= 𝛥𝐾𝐸. Assume the puck starts at rest.

answer.html: Karl's air does positive work 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑 on the puck. The bar graph shows 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>= 0, plus a work bar 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑, equals a final bar 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝐹𝑑 of the same height. The puck's kinetic energy increases by exactly the work done.

items.title: 4b. Puck with half the mass, same force and distance

body.html: 𝑊= 𝐹𝑑 is unchanged. So 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝑊 is also unchanged. With half the mass, 𝑣= √2𝐾𝐸/ 𝑚 is larger by √2 ≈1.41.

answer.html: The work done and the final kinetic energy are the same as in part a; only the puck's speed is greater (by a factor of 1.41).

items.title: 4c. Describe parts a and b in terms of impulse and momentum

body.html: Impulse = 𝐹𝛥𝑡= 𝛥𝑝, and 𝑝= √2𝑚𝐾𝐸. For the same 𝐾𝐸, the half-mass puck has 𝑝 smaller by √1 / 2. It accelerates at twice the rate, so it covers the distance in a time shorter by 1 / √2 .

answer.html: In both parts the force is the same, but the lighter puck is pushed for a shorter time (𝛥𝑡 smaller by a factor 1 / √2 ). The impulse 𝐹𝛥𝑡 and the final momentum are therefore smaller by 1 / √2 ≈0.71 for the lighter puck, even though the final kinetic energy is the same.
